kicker: UI SDK, read from the code

scenes.text: An agent can write a select that looks perfect. Why do its arrow keys do nothing?
scenes.say: An agent can write a select that looks perfect. So why do its arrow keys do nothing?

scenes.headline: How UI SDK lets agents build and drive interfaces
scenes.sub: Behaviors to compose, and a bridge to operate the result
scenes.say: Hi, I'm Linnea! Vercel's UI SDK is not a generative UI runtime. It is behaviors for agents to build with, and a bridge for agents to use the result.

scenes.title: Behaviors, not looks
scenes.sub: The look is easy. The keys are not.

steps.say: Vercel's launch video takes a select apart. Arrow keys through a list. Typing to jump ahead. Remembering the choice.
Each piece is a behavior: popup, listbox, typeahead, selection. A model gets the box and the chevron right. It gets these wrong.

steps.term: Behavior: one job an interface does
steps.say: At the bottom, a kernel: a state store, parts, and change details. On top, the behaviors, one job each, like roving focus or a popup.
A primitive puts one component together: its state, the API that changes it, and its parts. No markup, no styles.
Adapters render it in React, Vue, Svelte, Solid or web components. You write the markup and styles.

steps.note: the shipped components use the same public behaviors
steps.say: The shipped components use the same behaviors, so a component an agent writes gets the same keyboard support.
The README's search field has a name and one piece of state, the value.

steps.term: API: the only way state changes
steps.say: The API is the only way that state changes. It is what the agent will call later.
The clear button is a slot. It exists only while there is text, and pressing it empties the value.
The intended workflow: ask for a teammate picker, and the agent composes four behaviors into one primitive.

scenes.title: Driving the page
scenes.sub: Three tools instead of a screenshot

steps.term: Agent bridge: three tools over the page
steps.say: The bridge gives a model three tools. Snapshot lists the page. Act runs steps. Query finds a component or a list item.
Every component registers itself as it is made, with a ref, its accessible name, its state and its actions.
Act calls the component's own API. Your change callback hears it, tagged with source agent, and can cancel it.

params.left: Browser tools: look, click, look again
status: Snapshot names each control and gives it a ref.
A browser agent finds each control by looking, clicks, and reads the page again.
The bridge sends all four steps in one call, straight to each API.
Nothing to re-read. On another task, the docs measured 16 calls against 5.

steps.say: Take the video's task: Asia Pacific, the Pro plan, three instances, preview deployments on. Snapshot first gives each control a ref.
A browser agent finds each control by looking, clicks it, then reads the page again. Field after field.
The bridge sends all four steps in one act call, each through the control's own API.
Act returns every value, so nothing is read twice. The docs measured sixteen tool calls against five, on a different task.

scenes.title: The same task in the launch video

steps.say: In the launch video, each phrase lights up as its control changes. Four settings changed.

scenes.title: How a step finds its component

steps.say: A step can name a component in words, like Jane Doe. But anyone can write page text. Is it a ref? No.

steps.term: Row text: words beside a control
steps.say: Labels and row text: a checkbox labelled Jane Doe matches, and so does an Admin menu on her row. An exact label does not win.
A tie narrows to components that take the action. Press passes for all of them.
So the step is refused, listing both refs. The agent must pick one on purpose.

scenes.title: A person in the loop
scenes.say: Chapter three. A person in the loop.

scenes.title: Marks in plain HTML
scenes.say: Three HTML attributes decide what an agent may do alone. People see no difference.

items.say: Confirm carries a sentence. Without an allow callback the step fails. With one, it waits for the person.
Hidden removes a region from what the agent can see at all.
Secret lets the agent type into a field, but never read it back.
And every agent change reaches your callbacks tagged as the agent's.

steps.say: The docs' one benchmark: browser tools on another library against the bridge. Fewer calls, less text, less time.
Medians of three runs, the other library unnamed, no harness in the repo. I believe the direction, not the size.

scenes.title: Where it stops
scenes.say: The code also shows the limits.

items.say: Snapshot lists only UI SDK components. A plain button or a bare input is invisible to the agent.
A failed step stops the call with no rollback, and ok can be true while a callback cancelled the change.

items.text: Beta, under three weeks of history
items.say: And it is a beta, with under three weeks of commit history and three human authors.

scenes.text: Don't make an agent reverse-engineer your interface from pixels. Hand it the API the interface already has.
scenes.say: An agent driving a page by screenshots is reverse engineering an API the app already has. UI SDK hands it that API.

recap: Snapshot, act and query, no screenshots
scenes.say: To recap. Behaviors for agents to compose. A bridge that drives the page through its own API. And names treated as untrusted page text.
